readings.title: First reading
readings.text:
The Lord has pitilessly destroyed
all the homes of Jacob;
in his displeasure he has shattered
the strongholds of the daughter of Judah;
he has thrown to the ground,
he has left accursed the kingdom and its rulers.
Mutely they sit on the ground,
the elders of the daughter of Zion;
they have put dust on their heads,
and wrapped themselves in sackcloth.
The virgins of Jerusalem hang their heads
down to the ground.
My eyes wasted away with weeping,
my entrails shuddered,
my liver spilled on the ground
at the ruin of the daughters of my people,
as children, mere infants, fainted
in the squares of the Citadel.
They kept saying to their mothers,
‘Where is the bread?’
as they fainted like wounded men
in the squares of the City,
as they poured out their souls
on their mothers’ breasts.
How can I describe you, to what compare you,
daughter of Jerusalem?
Who can rescue and comfort you,
virgin daughter of Zion?
For huge as the sea is your affliction;
who can possibly cure you?
The visions your prophets had on your behalf
were delusive, tinsel things,
they never pointed out your sin,
to ward off your exile.
The visions they proffered you were false,
fallacious, misleading.
Cry aloud, then, to the Lord,
groan, daughter of Zion;
let your tears flow like a torrent,
day and night;
give yourself no relief,
grant your eyes no rest.
Up, cry out in the night-time,
in the early hours of darkness;
pour your heart out like water
before the Lord.
Stretch out your hands to him
for the lives of your children
who faint with hunger
at the entrance to every street.

exegesis.summary: Jeremiah's lament surveys the rubble of Jerusalem: temple razed, elders silent in dust, infants dying for want of bread in their mothers' arms. The prophet does not soften the blow—he names false prophets who flattered the people instead of exposing their sin. Yet the lament ends not in despair but in command: pour out your heart like water before the Lord and stretch out your hands for the lives of your children.

patristicQuotes.quote: By Jerusalem He means not the stones and buildings, but the dwellers there, over whom He laments with the feeling of a Father.

I do not deny that the former Jerusalem was destroyed because of the wickedness of its inhabitants, but the weeping might also concern this your spiritual Jerusalem. For if a man has sinned after receiving the mysteries of truth, he will be wept over.

cccReferences.title: Israel's eventual recognition of the Messiah

exegesis.thematicConnection: The ruined Daughter of Zion sets the stage for the Gospel, where the true King enters not Jerusalem but Capernaum, and where it is a Gentile soldier—not the chosen city—who shows the faith that could have spared Israel's downfall.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
Do not forget your poor servants for ever.
Why, O God, have you cast us off for ever?
Why blaze with anger at the sheep of your pasture?
Remember your people whom you chose long ago,
the tribe you redeemed to be your own possession,
the mountain of Zion where you made your dwelling.
Do not forget your poor servants for ever.
Turn your steps to these places that are utterly ruined!
The enemy has laid waste the whole of the sanctuary.
Your foes have made uproar in your house of prayer:
they have set up their emblems, their foreign emblems,
high above the entrance to the sanctuary.
Do not forget your poor servants for ever.
Their axes have battered the wood of its doors.
They have struck together with hatchet and pickaxe.
O God, they have set your sanctuary on fire:
they have razed and profaned the place where you dwell.
Do not forget your poor servants for ever.
Remember your covenant; every cave in the land
is a place where violence makes its home.
Do not let the oppressed return disappointed;
let the poor and the needy bless your name.
Do not forget your poor servants for ever.
readings.refrain: Do not forget your poor servants for ever.

exegesis.summary: The psalmist takes Jeremiah's grief and turns it into prayer, naming the desecration of the sanctuary and pleading that God remember His covenant. The refrain anchors the whole cry: 'Do not forget your poor servants for ever.' Even amid ruin, the people refuse to let go of their identity as the flock of God's pasture.

patristicQuotes.quote: It is possible even for the dweller in Jerusalem to incur guilt, and even the most richly endowed may stray. And unless these repent speedily, they lose the capacity wherewith they were endued.

cccReferences.title: Prayer in the shadow of the Temple
All troubles summed up in the cry of the Word
God hears the cry of the poor

exegesis.thematicConnection: The psalm gives voice to the prayer Lamentations demands, and prepares us for the centurion who likewise pours out his heart for one who suffers—'do not forget your poor servant'—and is heard at once.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text:
When Jesus went into Capernaum a centurion came up and pleaded with him. ‘Sir,’ he said ‘my servant is lying at home paralysed, and in great pain.’ ‘I will come myself and cure him’ said Jesus. The centurion replied, ‘Sir, I am not worthy to have you under my roof; just give the word and my servant will be cured. For I am under authority myself, and have soldiers under me; and I say to one man: Go, and he goes; to another: Come here, and he comes; to my servant: Do this, and he does it.’ When Jesus heard this he was astonished and said to those following him, ‘I tell you solemnly, nowhere in Israel have I found faith like this. And I tell you that many will come from east and west to take their places with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob at the feast in the kingdom of heaven; but the subjects of the kingdom will be turned out into the dark, where there will be weeping and grinding of teeth.’ And to the centurion Jesus said, ‘Go back, then; you have believed, so let this be done for you.’ And the servant was cured at that moment.
He took our sicknesses away and carried our diseases for us.

exegesis.summary: A Roman centurion intercedes for his paralyzed servant with a faith so pure that Jesus marvels: 'Nowhere in Israel have I found faith like this.' His confession—'Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word'—becomes the Church's own prayer at every Mass. Jesus then warns that many will come from east and west to feast with the patriarchs while the heirs of the kingdom are cast out, and He fulfills Isaiah: 'He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.'

patristicQuotes.quote: This centurion was the first-fruits of the Gentiles, and in comparison of his faith all the faith of the Jews was unbelief; he neither heard Christ teaching nor saw the leper cleansed, but from hearing only that He had healed, he believed more than he heard.

As we commend the centurion's faith in that he believed the Saviour was able to heal the paralytic, so his humility is seen in his professing himself unworthy that the Lord should come under his roof.

exegesis.thematicConnection: Where Lamentations mourns a faithless Jerusalem fed by false visions, the Gospel reveals a pagan soldier whose true vision of Christ's authority secures the healing Israel forfeited—the very reversal the lament warned was coming.

synthesis.title: From the rubble of Zion to the Lord's table—faith finds its true home
synthesis.body: Today the Church holds together two scenes that, on the surface, could not be more different: Jerusalem reduced to ashes, mothers cradling fainting children in the streets, and a Roman officer in Capernaum kneeling before Jesus for a dying servant. But Lamentations and the Gospel tell one story. Jerusalem fell because her prophets gave her 'delusive, tinsel' visions instead of naming her sin; the centurion, with no Law and no Prophets, sees clearly who Jesus is and speaks the truth: 'Only say the word.' The psalmist's refrain—'Do not forget your poor servants for ever'—becomes flesh in the centurion's plea for his paralyzed slave, and Christ does not forget. He marvels at this Gentile faith and announces that many will come from east and west to recline at the feast of Abraham, while those who presumed on their inheritance may be cast out. The Church places the centurion's words on our lips before every Communion: Domine, non sum dignus. Today she invites us to choose which Jerusalem we will be—the city that trusted flattering visions, or the soul that, knowing its unworthiness, simply trusts the Word. Only the second will sit at the banquet that has no end.
